caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 60 of 2011
lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Senior Advocate instructed by Syed Mahbubar Rahman Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners. 
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate instructed by Gias Uddin  Ahmed Advocate-on-Record ------ For Respondent Nos. 1,2, 4, 6 and 46. 
None Respondent ------ For Respondent Nos. 3, 5, 7-45, 47-63.
parties:
Abdur Rahman Pramanik (Md) and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Alefa Bewa and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the18th day of April, 2010 pass by the High Court Division, in civil Revision No. 3506 of 2007).
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J : This petition for leave to appeal is from the judgment and order dated 18-4-2010 and 19-4-2010 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3506 of 2007 discharging the Rule.

2. Facts emerged from the judgment of the Appellate Court, the impugned judgment and order and the leave petition are that Halimon Bibi, predecessor-in-interest of the respondents as the plaintiff filed Partition Suit No.141 of 1962 in the Court of Sub or din ate Judge, Bogra (Now the Joint District Judge, First Court, Bogra) for partition of the suit land.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No.1, Ositullah @ Dasham Tullah Fakir, by filing a written statement.

4. At the trial, both parties adduced evidence. On conclusion of hearing of the suit, the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 22-6-1964 decreed the suit in preliminary form on contest against defendant No.1 and ex-parte against the other defendants. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, defendant No.1, Ositullah Fakir, filed Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 in the Court of District Judge, Bogra. The predecessor of the petitioners also filed Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964. During the pendency of the appeals, on 24-2-1969, the plaintiff-respondent filed an application in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 for withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh on the ground of formal defect. The learned District Judge, Bogra by the order dated 24-2-1969 allowed the application and thereby the suit stood withdrawn. Long after 33 years of the said order of withdrawal of the suit, the plaintiff-Halimon Bibi on 6-1-2002 filed an application in the trial Court for passing final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree dated 22-6-1964 and accordingly, a survey knowing Advocate was appointed as Commissioner who submitted his report, the report was accepted and the final decree was passed on 4-5-2002; the final decree was sealed and signed on 9-5-2004. Subsequently, the final decree was put into execution through Execution Case No. 1 of 2002.

5. The petitioners having known about the said final decree filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) and section 44 of the Evidence Act for setting aside the final decree dated 4-5-2002 on the ground that the same was obtained fraudulently by suppressing the fact that the suit was withdrawn by the order of the learned District Judge dated 24-2- 1969 on the ground of formal defect and, in fact after withdrawal of the suit, there was no preliminary decree and also prayed for staying all further proceedings of the execution case till the hearing of the application. And all further proceedings of the execution case were stayed:

Eventually, the application was allowed by the order dated 14-10-2002 and the execution case was postponed. Being aggrieved by the said order, the plaintiff-Halimon Bibi filed Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003 before the High Court Division. A learned Judge of the Single Bench by the judgment and order dated 11-1-2004 made the Rule absolute, set aside order dated 14-10-2002 passed by the trial Court on the view that "since the suit has been finally disposed of-with the signing and sealing of the final decree, such decree can not be disturbed on an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thus the impugned order is not sustainable in law and liable to be set aside." The learned Judge further observed that "it appears that against the final decree there are specific provision for appeal the applicant if aggrieved have to avail such remedy by way of appeal against the final decree since the decree can be challenged in an appeal and the aggrieved party has other remedy available, the inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be invoked."

6. The defendants did not challenge the said judgment and order of the High Court Division before this Court and as per observations made therein filed Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004 before the District Judge, Bogra against the final decree. The learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra on hearing the appeal by the judgment and decree dated 25-6-2007 dismissed the appeal. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge, the petitioners filed Civil Revision No.2506 of 2007 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule. The revision was heard by the same learned Judge who earlier disposed Civil Revision No.106 of 2003 and he, by the impugned judgment and order (dated 18-4-2010 and 19-4- 2010), discharged the Rule; hence this petition for leave to appeal.

7. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Counsel for the petitioners, has submitted that after the withdrawal of the suit by the plaintiff in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964, there was no existence of the preliminary decree passed in the suit by the trial Court. Therefore, the final decree passed pursuant to the preliminary decree was without jurisdiction, but the learned Additional District Judge as well as the learned Judge of the High Court Division failed to consider that simple factual and legal aspect of the case and thus fell into an error in maintaining the final decree passed in the suit and, as such, the impugned judgment and order calls for interference by this Court by way of granting leave.

8. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel entering caveat on behalf of respondent Nos. 1, 2, 4, 6, and 46, on the other hand, has supported the impugned judgment and order and has made submission to dismiss the leave petition.

9. Mr Abdul Quayum has placed the judgment and order passed in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003, the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 15 of 2004, the orders passed by the learned District Judge in Partition Appeal Nos. 13 and 8 of 1964 and the impugned judgment and order.

<u>10. In the facts and circumstances of the case as stated hereinabove, two interesting questions are to be decided in this petition: (a) whether after withdrawal of the suit at the appellate stage, the preliminary decree passed in the withdrawn suit could be the basis for passing final decree and if any final decree passed any how in the context could be put into execution, (b) whether, in the instant appeal (Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004) giving rise to the instant revision (Civil Revision No. 3506 of 2007), the Additional District Judge could sit over the order passed by the District Judge in the earlier appeal being Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 allowing the plaintiff-respondent to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh on the view that the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 was not legal and defective.</u>

11. To answer the questions, the most relevant materials to be considered are the two orders passed in Partition Appeal Nos. 13 of 1964 and 8 of 1964. With the additional paper book, the entire order sheets of the two partition appeals (Nos. 8 of 1964 and 13 of 1964) have been filed. From the order sheets of the two appeals, it appears that, in fact, the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh was passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964. The order of withdrawal of the suit was passed on 24-2-1969

The order reads as follows:

Respondent I entered appearance today. The appeal is taken up for hearing. Argument at length heard on both sides. Respondent at the close of the argument files application praying for withdrawal of the original Part. Suit with leave to sue afresh on grounds of formal defects. The suit, especially law to the amendment allowed at day end of the trial for formal defect since the prayer for withdrawal of the suit should be allowed. The court fees paid is sufficient. Hence it is

Order

That the plff respondent be permitted to withdraw the suit with liberty to bring a fresh suit if not otherwise barred. In view of the withdrawal of the suit there stand no decree and therefore there is no locus standi for the appeal which therefore is accordingly disposed of.”

12. From the order sheets of Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964, it appears that the argument in the appeal was heard on 8-2-1969 and the judgment was reserved till hearing of Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 and on 24-2-1696 i.e. the date on which the order was passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh the following order was passed in that appeal (8 of 1964)

"The original part, suit has been withdrawn by the plaintiff respondent in PA 13/64. The suit having been withdrawn there is no scope for this appeal which therefore be accordingly disposed of."

<u>13. From the two orders passed in the two appeals as quoted hereinbefore, it is clear that the plaintiffs suit for partition stood withdrawn on 24-2-1969 and with the withdrawal of the suit, the preliminary decree passed therein became non existent or non-est, even then in the order permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to suit afresh, it was specifically stated "I n view of the withdrawal of the suit there stand no decree. "And because of withdrawal of the suit, the appeals were not disposed of on merit. Against the order of withdrawal of the suit, the plaintiff did not take any step to set aside the order either on the ground of fraud or on any other illegality or irregularity, but after 33 years of the said order on 6-1-2002 filed on application in the suit to pass final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree though there was no existence of any preliminary decree on that date and the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra appointed an Advocate Commissioner to give saham to the plaintiff according to the preliminary decree, who submitted his report and on acceptance of the Commissioner's report submitted on 22-4-2002, passed the final decree 4-5-2002 and the final decree was sealed and signed on 9-5-2002 and then Execution Case No. 1 of 2002 was filed on 16-5-2002 for execution of the final decree.</u>

14. As quoted hereinbefore, the Rule in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003 was made absolute on two grounds: (i) against the final decree, there was specific provision for appeal and if the defendants were, in fact, aggrieved, they had to avail such remedy by way of filing an appeal, (ii) since the final decree had been sealed and signed, the application under section 151 of the Code was not maintainable.

15. In the context, it needs to be mentioned that in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003, the learned Judge of the Single Bench did not say anything about the propriety of the order passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission of sue afresh. It is also an admitted fact that pursuant to the observations made by the learned Judge in the said civil revision (Civil Revision No. 106 of 2006), the defendants preferred Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004 before the District Judge, Bogra. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra and he dismissed the appeal on the findings, inter alia, that on examining the application filed for withdrawal of the suit, it appeared that there was no signature of Halimon Bibi and there was also no verification in the application; that the order dated 24-2-1969 allowing plaintiff-respondent No.1 to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh was passed through inadvertence and before passing the order no statement of the plaintiff-respondent to the effect that there was formal defect in the main suit was recorded which was logical and legal requirement, that the order permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit was not legal and was defective.

16. The learned Additional District Judge in his penultimate finding held that the order dated 24-2-1969 passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 being a defective order from the legal point of view, there was no logic to maintain that order and therefore, it could not be said that there was no existence of the preliminary decree dated 22-6-1964. The learned Additional District Judge further held that since the preliminary decree was passed in the suit on detailed discussion and the lower Court did not give any finding that there was defect in the framing of the suit; there was no scope to withdraw the suit on the ground of formal defect, the final decree was rightly passed on 4-5-2002 on the basis of the application filed by the plaintiff pursuant to the preliminary decree.

17. The learned Additional District Judge observed that there was no straight order setting aside the preliminary decree in Partition Appeal Nos. 13 of 1964 and 8 of 1964 and in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003, in fact, the preliminary decree and the final decree were confirmed. The learned Additional District Judge further observed that since defendant Nos. 9-11 and 15 did not contest the suit and the decree was passed against them ex-parte, they had no locus standi to file Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964. The learned Additional District Judge further held that since defendant Nos. 9-11 and IS did not file any objection against the Advocate Commissioner's report the instant appeal (Appeal No. 15 of 2004) at their instance was not maintainable in law.

18. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the learned Judge of the Single Bench simply dittoed the view of the learned Additional District Judge, but in different language. However, the learned Judge added a new finding that the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh was obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court, and the reason in finding so were that in the application for withdrawal, there was neither any signature of the plaintiff nor there was any verification or affidavit as required under rule 19 of the Civil Rules and Orders and under Order VI, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and that there was nothing on record to show that either summons of Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 was served upon the plaintiff-Halimon Bibi or she appeared in the said appeal. The learned Judge gave further finding that Title Appeal No.8 of 1964 was an independent appeal and though no application for withdrawal of the suit was filed by the plaintiff in that appeal, the order was passed withdrawing the suit.

19. In the above back drop, keeping in view the findings of the Court below and the learned Judge of the High Court Division, let us examine the two questions as formulated hereinbefore.

20. One thing is absolutely clear that the orders passed by the learned District Judge in Partition Appeal Nos.13 of 1964 and 8 of 1964 were very much in force with all their legal implication on the date of filing the application by the plaintiff on 6-1-2002 for passing the final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree and till date, those are in force with the same legal implication as stood on 6-1-2002. It is also a fact that the defendants in their application under section 151 of the Code along with section 44 of the Evidence Act categorically stated about the said fact of withdrawal of the suit by the plaintiff and the order passed by the Appellate Court. But the plaintiff as well as her heirs after her death did not take any step either to vacate or set aside the order. In the context, it is also necessary to state that the learned Additional District Judge gave finding that the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh was defective from the legal point of view and there was no logic to maintain that order, but he failed to consider that the date on which the application for passing the final decree was filed, the date on which the Advocate Commissioner was appointed to give the saham, the date of submission of the report by the Advocate Commissioner arid the passing of the final decree, the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh had all its legal implication and by no legal fiction, the trial Court could ignore that.

21. Be that as it may, the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh having been passed in a completely separate appeal being Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964, we failed to understand under what provision of law the learned Additional District Judge and the High Court Division sat over the order passed in that appeal. So long the order dated 24-2-1969 passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 remained in force, neither the learned Additional District Judge nor the learned Judge of the High Court Division could by-pass or ignore the same as has been done by them.

<u>22. The learned Additional District Judge did not find any fraud in the order dated 24-2-1969 in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 passed by the learned District Judge, what he found, was that the order was not legal and defective. But the learned Judge of the High Court Division found that the order withdrawing the suit was obtained fraudulently. Fraud is basically a question of fact and that has to be alleged by a party and, if alleged, the other side has to be given chance to controvert such facts, but in the instant case, no such allegation was made either by the plaintiff or by her heirs after her death. As stated earlier, neither the plaintiff nor her heirs ever made any application before the District Judge, Bogra to set aside the order dated 24-6-1969 alleging fraud in obtaining the order, because the order having been passed by the learned District Judge, only he could set aside or vacate the order if it could be established that the order was obtained by practising fraud upon him.</u>

23. From the judgment of the Appellate Court (Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004), it further appears that the plaintiff-respondent claimed that she did not put her signature or left thumb impression in any application for withdrawal of the suit on the ground of formal defect or in the verification in support of the application, but she did not say that no application for withdrawal was filed by her learned Advocated and no allegation was also made that the application for withdrawal was filed by her learned Advocate in collusion with the learned Advocate of the other side or the appellants or that she never engaged any Advocate to appear on her behalf or that the learned Advocate who filed the application was not at all engaged by her or that she did not enter appearance in the appeal through the learned Advocate on 24-2-1969 who filed the application for withdrawal of the suit or that her learned Advocate did not participate in the hearing of the appeal (in the order dated 24-2-1969, it has been clearly stated that "Respondent No.1 entered appearance today. The appeal is taken up for hearing. Argument at length heard on both sides"). So, the question of obtaining the order dated 24-2-1969 by practising fraud as found by the learned Judge of the High Court Division does not arise at all.

24. From the above, it is clear that the plaintiff who was respondent No.1 appeared in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 and because of the order permitting him to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh, the appeal was not disposed of on merit and for the same reason Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 was also not disposed of on merit. The application for making the preliminary decree final was filed long after 33 years, is it believable that when the plaintiff appeared in the appeal through her learned Advocate and the appeal was not disposed of on merit, she would not know about the disposal of the appeal, or keep any information about the appeal and so also the order of withdrawal of the suit, even if for argument's sake, it is accepted that in the application for withdrawal of the suit, she did not put any signature or left thumb impression and that the application was not verified by her and that before passing the order, her statement was not recorded.

<u>25. Similarly had the suit giving rise to the appeals not been withdrawn, defendant No.1 and the other defendants who filed the appeals would not sit idle. More so, had the suit not been withdrawn, the appeals would have been disposed of in some way, i.e. either on merit or by default, but nothing happened. Be that as it may, in no way, the learned Additional District Judge could sit suo moto over the order passed by the learned District Judge in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh. The moment the suit stood withdrawn and the Appellate Court passed order to the effect "there stand no decree" by no legal fiction, the preliminary decree passed in the suit could be said or treated to be in existence and as such, no application could be filed to pass the final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree and for that matter to proceed under the provisions of Order XXVI, rules 13 and 14 of the Code. In other words, rightly or wrongly when the Appellate Court passed the order permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh in the terms as quoted hereinbefore, there was no scope to say that the preliminary decree remained in existence after 24-2-1969, inasmuch as with the withdrawal of the suit whatever may be the preliminary decree passed therein became non existent and non-est. suit unfortunately, the learned Additional District Judge and the learned Judge of the High Court Division did not at all consider these factual and legal aspects of the case in maintaining the final decree passed on the non existent and non-est preliminary decree. Further, the lower Court's records were sent to the District Judge in connection with Partition Appeal Nos. 8 and 13 of 1964 as clearly noted in the orders dated 22-12-1964 and 27-3-1965 respectively passed in the appeals and after the disposal of the appeals, the records must have been sent to the lower Court and the result of the appeal must have also been communicated to the trial Court, but in acting on the application of the plaintiff to pass final decree pursuant to the non-est preliminary decree, the trial Court did not at all look at the order passed by the Appellate Court.</u>

26. Now, the finding or the High Court Division that "the suit or an appeal is independent and should be independently determined", but no application for withdrawal of the suit was filed by the plaintiff in Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 and that it did not find any service of notice of the appeal either upon the plaintiff or any other respondents. The finding of the High Court Division as to the non service of notice of appeal upon the plaintiff-respondent and' the other respondents is prima facie wrong, as order No. 3 of Title Appeal No. 8 of 1964 shows that notice of the appeal were served upon all the respondents. Order No. 3 reads as follows:

"Notices served upon all the respondents (respondents included principal and proforma-respondents) they do not appear. Court guardian of minor respondents 5 to 7 also does not apear. LCR not received. Issue this appeal." a reminder. To 22-12-1964 for LCR and order

The next order (Order No.4) dated 22-12- 1964 reads as follows:

"LCR received. To 26-3-1964 for settling the date of hearing."

27. Reading order Nos. 3 and 4 together, it is prima facie clear that notices of the appeal were duly served upon the respondents and after the receipt of the lower Court's records, the appeal was set for settling the date of hearing and it was heard on 8-6-1969. Thus it is clear that the appeal was not heard abruptly or without any notice upon the plaintiff who was allegedly made proforma defendant No.17 (as found by the High Court Division). Furthermore, the plaintiff never made any complaint either in the instant appeal (Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004) or in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003 that notice of Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 was not served upon her or she had no knowledge of the said appeal. In the context, it is very pertinent to state that after the service of notice of the appeal, option was with the plaintiff-respondent either to appear in the appeal or not. The High Court Division was also wrong in finding fault with the order of withdrawal or the suit on the ground that no application for withdrawal was filed in Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964, because. both the appeals were filed against the judgment and decree passed in one suit being Partition Suit No.141 of 1962, so it was not necessary to file separate application in Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964, when application was filed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964. And, in fact, no 'order for withdrawal of the suit was passed in, this appeal. From the order dated 24-2-1969 (the order has been quoted earlier), it is also clear that this appeal (Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964) was disposed with the observation that since the original partition suit had been withdrawn by the plaintiff-respondent in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964, there was no scope "for this appeal."

<u>28. The learned Additional District Judge and the High Court Division were also totally wrong in taking the view that since the appellants did not contest the partition suit by filing written statement, they could not file Title Appeal No. 8 of 1964, inasmuch as it is a well settled legal proposition that even if a 3rd party is affected by a decree, he can file an appeal against such decree and in the instant case, the appellants very much were parties to the suit. The only bar put by the legislature in a suit for partition as in section 97 of the Code is that where any party aggrieved by a preliminary decree does not appeal from such decree, he shall be precluded from disputing its correctness in any appeal which may be preferred from the final. decree. This bar was not applicable in, the instant case, as the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 8 of 1964 before the District Judge against the preliminary decree and that appeal was not disposed of on merit on the ground that the suit out of which the appeal arose, had been withdrawn, so the instant appeal by the defendants against the final decree was quite competent and maintainable.</u>

29. The learned Additional District Judge and the High Court Division were also wrong in not entertaining the appeal on the ground that the defendants did not file any objection against the Advocate Commissioner's report inasmuch as there being no existence of the preliminary decree in the eye of law, the very appointment of the Advocate Commissioner to give saham to the plaintiff pursuant to the preliminary decree was without jurisdiction. Furthermore, in the application filed by the petitioners under section 151 of the Code before the trial Court to set aside the final decree, it was categorically stated that the plaintiff by suppressing the fact of withdrawal of the suit on 24-2-1969 filed the application for, making the preliminary decree final and by practising fraud upon the, Court and in a hurried manner made the non existent preliminary decree final on 4-5-2002 and the decree was sealed and signed on 9-5-2002, so there was no scope of filing the objection against the Commissioner's report.

<u>30. Now, the other 'legal questions which have to be addressed are whether the application for withdrawal of the suit was required to be signed by the plaintiff-respondent, whether the same also was required to be verified by her or supported by an affidavit and whether the statements of the plaintiff was needed to be recorded before passing the order allowing her to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh as held by the Appellate Court as well as by the High Court Division.</u>

<u>31. Rule 14 of Order VI of the Code has clearly provided that every pleading shall be signed by the party and his pleader (if any). The rule also provides that where a party pleading is, by reason of absence or for other good cause, unable to sign the pleading, it may be signed by any person duly authorized by him to sign the same or to sue or defend on his behalf. Rule 15(1) of Order VI has provided that save as otherwise provided by any law for the time being in force, every pleading shall be verified at the foot by the party or by one of the parties pleading or by some other person proved to the satisfaction of the Court to be acquainted with the facts of the case. (Sub-rules (2) and (3) of rule 15 are not relevant for the present purpose). And according to rule 1 of Order VI "pleading" shall mean plaint or written statement. So, by no stretch of imagination, the application for withdrawal of a suit can be treated or termed as pleading. Therefore, we do not see the requirement of verification in the application for withdrawal of a suit as found by the learned Additional District Judge and the learned Judge of the High Court Division. In this regard, it may be also stated that the applications/petitions which would require affidavit in support of the prayer made therein have been specifically mentioned in the Code such as, prayer for attachment before judgment under Order XXVIII, rule 5, prayer for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rule 1 of the Code. But nowhere in Order XXIII, sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 1, which have dealt with withdrawal of suit or abandonment of part of claim the phraseology "affidavit" has been referred to or mentioned, when the Code is silent about the necessity or requirement of any verification or affidavit to make a prayer for withdrawal of a suit, the Court could not impose such a condition to file an application for withdrawal of a suit. So, the Appellate Court and the High Court Division were apparently wrong in finding that the application for withdrawal of the suit in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 was defective as the same was not verified by the plaintiff or supported by any affidavit.</u>

<u>32. The learned Additional District Judge as well as the High Court Division found the order dated 24-2-1969 defective on the ground that the application for withdrawal of the suit was not signed by the plaintiff-respondent, Halimon Bibi. As already found hereinbefore, the application for withdrawal of a suit need not be verified by the plaintiff and that need not be signed by the plaintiff as well and it was enough if the same was filed by her learned Advocate. Admittedly, the application for withdrawal was filed by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent. An Advocate (in the Code still it is pleader) is the attorney of the plaintiff or the defendant as the case may be and he is legally quite competent to file any application in the suit including the application for withdrawal of a suit. In rule 1 of Order Ill of the Code, it has been clearly provided that any appearance, application or act in or to any Court required or authorized by law to be made or done by a party in such Court, may, except where otherwise expressly provided by any law for the time being in force; be made or done by the party in person, or by his recognized agent, or by a pleader appearing, applying or acting, as the case may be, on his behalf: provided that any such appearance shall, if the Court so directs, be made by the partly in person. In the context rule 4 of the order is very relevant and I consider it better to quote the rule in its entirety which is as under:</u>

<u>"4.(1) No pleader shall act for any person in any Court, unless he has been appointed for the purpose by such person by a document in writing signed by such person or by his recognized agent or by some other person duly authorized by or under a power-of- attorney to make such appointment.</u>

<u>(2) Every such appointment shall be filed in Court and shall be deemed to be in force until determined with the leave of the Court by a writing signed by the client or the pleader, as the case may be, and filed in Court, or until the client or the pleader dies, or until all proceedings in the suit are ended so far as regards the client.</u>

<u>(3) For the purposes of sub-rule (2) an application for review of judgment, an application under section 144 or section 152 of this Code, any appeal from any decree or order in the suit and any application or act for the purpose of obtaining copies of documents or return of documents produced or filed in the suit or of obtaining refund of monies paid into the Court in connection with the suit shall be deemed to be proceedings in the suit.</u>

<u>(4) The High Court Division may, by general order, direct that, where the person by whom a pleader is appointed is unable to write his name, his mark upon the document appointing the pleader shall be attested by such person and in such manner as may' be specified by the order (5) No pleader who has been engaged for the purpose of pleading only shall plead on behalf of any party, unless he has filed in Court a memorandum of appearance signed by himself and stating-</u>

<u>(a) the names of the parties to the suit, (b) the name of the party for whom he appears, and</u>

<u>(c) the name of the person by whom he is authorized to appear.</u>

33. Provided that nothing in this sub-rule shall apply to any pleader engaged to plead on behalf of any party by any others pleader who has been duly appointed to act in Court on behalf of such party."

34. A reading of sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 4 shows that in order to act by an Advocate on behalf of a person a vokalatnama duly signed by him has to be filed and in the instant case as stated earlier the plaintiff-respondent did not deny the fact that she made appearance in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 through the learned Advocate who filed the application for withdrawal of the suit and in Order XXIII, sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 1, it has not been stated that the application for withdrawal of a suit either simpliciter or with permission to sue afresh has to be filed by the plaintiff himself (s). So, the learned Advocate who filed the vokalatnama on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent 'was quite competent to file the application for withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh and there was no necessity on the part of the plaintiff-respondent to sign the same and the learned District Judge rightly acted on it.

<u>35. Yet another legal point to be considered is whether, before passing the order allowing the application to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh, it was necessary to record the statement of the plaintiff-respondent that there was formal defect in the plaint for which she wanted to withdraw the suit. Rule 1 of Order XXIII of the Code reads as follows:</u>

<u>"1. (1) At any time after the institution of a suit the plaintiff may, as against all or any of the defendants, withdraw his suit or abandon</u>

<u>(2) Where the Court is satisfied-</u>

<u>(a) that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect, or</u>

<u>(b) that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject-matter of a suit or part of a claim, it may, on such terms as it thinks fit, grant the plaintiff permission to withdraw from such suit or abandon such part of a claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter of such suit or such part of a claim."</u>

36. In these two sub-rules, nothing has been said about the necessity of recording the statement of the plaintiff before according permission for withdrawing the suit either with permission to sue afresh or to withdraw a suit without permission to sue afresh. Only thing which has been provided in sub-rule (2) of rule 1 of Order XXIII is that in case of withdrawal of a suit with permission to sue afresh, the Court has to be satisfied that a suit must fail by reason of formal defect or that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of a suit or part of a claim. The satisfaction of the Court as spoken about in sub-rule (2) is relatable only to the question, there was some formal defect in farming of the suit for which the suit shall fail or that there are other sufficient grounds allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of a suit or part of claim, so the question of recording the statement of the plaintiff to the above effect as found by the learned District Judge and the High Court Division would not arise at all. It will not be out of context if we look at the provision of rule 3 of Order XXIII.

<u>37. This rule reads as follows:</u>

<u>"3. Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any law full agreement or compromise, or where the defendant satisfies the plaintiff in respect of the whole or any part of the subject-matter of the suit, the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded, and shall pass a decree to in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit."</u>

<u>38. A reading of this rule shows that before passing an order of agreement or recording a compromise, it has to be proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise. The phraseology used in this rule "Where it is proved to. the satisfaction of the Court" can very well be construed that to prove the satisfaction of the Court, as to the compromise of a suit, examination of the concerned party(s) is necessary, because the words "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court" cannot be confined or related to the filing of an application for compromise and it would need something more, i.e. before allowing the prayer under the rule, it has to be proved by the party(s) concerned that they really compromised the matter and the terms of compromise are lawful, but in case of an application for withdrawal of a suit, the phraseology "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court" has not been used. And it is being consistently followed by the Courts including the Apex Court (both the Divisions) that before recording compromise, the Court always examine the party(s) concerned to ascertain as to whether they really compromised the suit, as per terms of the solenama or the compromise petition, i.e. as per the language of the rule, whether a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise. But in sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 1, the phraseology "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court" being absent, it is only the satisfaction of the Court that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect or that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of a suit or part of a claim. And the learned District Judge having allowed the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh, it has to be presumed that he was satisfied as to the formal defect of the suit and in any view of the matter, the learned Additional District Judge was not legally empowered to question the satisfaction of the learned District Judge as to the formal defect of the suit in the instant appeal as that was not the lis before him. Therefore, the view taken by the learned Additional District Judge as well as the High Court Division that the recording of the statement of the plaintiff-respondent to the effect that there was formal defect which was a requirement of law and logical, so the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh was defective was absolutely erroneous.</u>

<u>39. For the discussions made hereinbefore, we are of the view that since there was no existence of any preliminary decree with the withdrawal of the suit, no final decree could be passed on a non-existent and non-est preliminary decree passed in the partition suit. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order calls for interference by this Court. And since both the parties have been well represented by their Senior Counsel, we consider it expedient to interfere with impugned judgment and order summarily without giving any leave, as if leave is granted, it would take long time to dispose of the matter and in the long run, it would endure to the sufferings of the parties. Since the cause of action for filing a suit for partition is recurring and the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh is still in force, the heirs of the deceased- plaintiff, Halimon Bibi, if so advised, can still file a suit for partition.</u>

Accordingly, the petition is disposed of in the following terms:

The impugned judgment and order affirming the judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra in Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004 and the final decree dated 4-5-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra (the decree drawn and signed on 9-5-2002) in Partition Suit No. 141 of 1962, are set aside. The heirs of the deceased-plaintiff, Halimon Bibi, if so advised, may file fresh suit for partition.

End.
